Foundations of Mechanical Ventilation

Build the mechanics vocabulary needed to understand how ventilators move gas, how compliance and resistance change airway pressures, how time constants shape filling and emptying, and how ventilator systems deliver a breath.

Why this foundation matters

Mechanical ventilation decisions can be lifesaving or harmful. Respiratory therapists are expected to recognize respiratory failure, select safe support, monitor the patient–ventilator system, manage and wean support, and prevent recurrence whenever possible.

1.2–1.3

Ventilation, respiration, and gas exchange

Ventilation is movement of air into and out of the lungs. Once gas reaches the alveoli, respiration describes movement of gas molecules across a cell membrane. External respiration occurs between the alveoli and pulmonary capillary blood; internal respiration occurs between systemic blood and tissue cells.

1.4–1.6

Airway pressures and pressure gradients

Air flows because a pressure difference exists. Gas moves from an area of higher pressure to an area of lower pressure, and flow reverses whenever the pressure gradient reverses.

Inspiration
Airway-opening pressure must be greater than alveolar pressure during positive-pressure inspiration, or alveolar pressure becomes subatmospheric during spontaneous inspiration.
Flow stops
Flow becomes zero when the pressures at both ends of the pathway equalize.
Expiration
Elastic recoil raises alveolar pressure above airway-opening pressure so gas exits the lungs.
1.7–1.8

Negative- and positive-pressure ventilation

Negative pressure

During normal spontaneous breathing, diaphragm contraction increases thoracic volume and lowers intrapleural and alveolar pressure. Air then moves from the atmosphere into the alveoli.

Positive pressure

A ventilator raises pressure at the airway opening. Gas enters until the cycle variable is reached, and expiration occurs as pressure falls and the respiratory system recoils toward baseline.

Historical media gap: The PDF references “Paul’s Story,” but the linked video is not included. The native lesson can use the current verified video link when supplied.
1.9–1.10

Pressure–time waveforms

The vertical axis represents pressure in cm H₂O and the horizontal axis represents time. A ventilator breath rises from baseline to peak inspiratory pressure (PIP). An inspiratory hold stops flow and reveals plateau pressure, which estimates alveolar pressure without the resistive pressure component. PEEP raises the expiratory baseline above zero and helps prevent complete alveolar collapse.

PIP
Total pressure needed to overcome elastic and resistive loads while gas is moving.
Plateau pressure
Pressure measured during an inspiratory hold when flow is zero.
PEEP
Positive pressure maintained at end expiration to keep alveoli from returning fully to zero pressure.
Patient effort
A negative deflection before a supported breath may represent the patient triggering the ventilator.
Workbook waveform challenge 12: spontaneous breath

Sketch alveolar pressure falling below zero during inspiration, returning to zero at the transition, then becoming positive during passive expiration before returning to baseline.

Workbook waveform challenge 16: PIP 30, plateau 20, PEEP 5, Ti 2 s, Te 4 s

Begin at PEEP 5, rise to PIP 30 by 2 seconds, perform an inspiratory hold at plateau 20, then return to PEEP and remain at baseline through the 4-second expiratory time. Total cycle time is 6 seconds, corresponding to 10 mandatory breaths/min.

Workbook waveform challenge 17: PIP 45, plateau 25, PEEP 10, Ti 1 s, Te 2 s, then a spontaneous breath

Begin at PEEP 10, rise to PIP 45, drop to plateau 25 during the hold, then return to PEEP across the 2-second expiratory phase. Add a spontaneous negative-pressure deflection below the same baseline. A 3-second mandatory cycle corresponds to 20 breaths/min; spontaneous breaths add to the total respiratory rate.

1.11–1.15

Compliance, elastance, and static compliance

Compliance describes how easily a structure distends; elastance describes its tendency to recoil toward its original shape. Stiff fibrotic lungs have low compliance, while emphysematous lungs may be overly compliant because elastic recoil has been lost.

CSTAT = Exhaled VT ÷ (Pplat − PEEP)
Use mL for tidal volume to report mL/cm H₂O. Plateau pressure is used because airflow is stopped during the inspiratory hold.
Source inconsistency flagged: One legacy example states Pplat 35 cm H₂O and PEEP 10 cm H₂O but shows 750 ÷ (27 − 10) = 44 mL/cm H₂O. This draft does not use that inconsistent worked example.

1.16–1.20

Airway resistance and regional lung units

Resistance represents frictional forces that must be overcome while gas is moving. Plateau pressure reflects the elastic pressure after flow stops; the difference between PIP and plateau pressure represents the pressure used to overcome airway resistance.

PTA = PIP − Pplat
Raw = (PIP − Pplat) ÷ Flow (L/s)
Larger diameter
Lower resistance and greater flow.
Smaller diameter
Higher resistance and reduced flow.
Artificial airway
An endotracheal or tracheostomy tube commonly adds a resistive pressure difference.

1.21–1.24

Time constants

A time constant combines compliance and resistance to estimate how quickly a lung unit fills and empties. Convert compliance to liters before multiplying so the units resolve to seconds.

Time constant = Compliance (L/cm H₂O) × Resistance (cm H₂O/L/s)
1 TC ≈ 63.2% filled · 2 TC ≈ 86.5% · 3 TC ≈ 95% · 4 TC ≈ 98.2% · 5 TC ≈ 99.3%
Short TC
Often reflects low compliance. The unit fills quickly but accepts less volume.
Normal TC
Allows effective filling and emptying within typical inspiratory and expiratory times.
Long TC
Often reflects high resistance. Slow emptying increases the risk of air trapping and auto-PEEP when expiratory time is too short.

Worked example: Compliance 25 mL/cm H₂O = 0.025 L/cm H₂O and Raw 30 cm H₂O/L/s. TC = 0.025 × 30 = 0.75 s. Three time constants are needed for approximately 95% inflation, so 0.75 × 3 = 2.25 seconds.

Increasing PIP with stable plateau
The resistive pressure difference is widening. Assess for bronchoconstriction, mucus, condensation, kinking, or artificial-airway obstruction.
PIP and plateau rise together
The elastic pressure is increasing, indicating worsening compliance. Protect the lung from excessive distending pressure and reassess the cause.

Chapter 2 essentials · applied equipment skills

How a ventilator works: set up, verify, and troubleshoot

Focus on the functional pathway you will use at the bedside: the ventilator conditions and delivers gas through the circuit, the patient exhales back through the circuit, and sensors confirm whether the machine, circuit, and patient agree.

Explore the system

Follow one breath through the ventilator

Inspiration: the ventilator regulates pressure, flow, volume, timing, and oxygen concentration, then sends conditioned gas through the inspiratory limb to the patient.
1
Power and gas sources

Confirm electrical power, battery status, and the required air and oxygen sources. A manual resuscitation device and backup oxygen must remain immediately available.

▣

Machine

Self-test passes, settings are correct, alarms are active, and monitored pressure, flow, volume, FiO₂, and PEEP are plausible.

⇄

Circuit

Connections are secure, tubing is unobstructed, filters and valves are oriented correctly, and condensation is controlled.

♥

Patient

Chest rise, breath sounds, synchrony, exhaled tidal volume, SpO₂, ETCO₂ when used, and clinical response match the displayed data.

The machine, circuit, and patient must agree. A powered-on screen does not prove that the patient is being ventilated effectively.

Before the patient is connected

Five-part pre-use verification

  1. Power and gases: verify electrical power, battery, oxygen, and compressed air when required.
  2. Correct circuit: inspect tubing, filters, humidification, valves, probes, and all connections.
  3. Automated test: complete the ventilator self-test, circuit leak test, and compliance compensation as required.
  4. Test lung: confirm delivered and exhaled pressure, flow, and volume before connecting the patient.
  5. Settings and safety: verify ordered settings, establish alarm limits, and keep a manual bag and backup oxygen ready.
Clinical practice

Troubleshoot by following the pathway

Patient→Airway→Connection→Circuit→Ventilator→Power & gases

Scenario 1 of 3

What students should know about ventilator power and internal mechanisms

Ventilators may use electricity, compressed gas, or both. Internal turbines, compressors, valves, pistons, or bellows create and regulate flow, but the bedside priority is functional: know what sources the device requires, what happens if a source fails, how to complete the manufacturer’s pre-use test, and how to provide immediate backup ventilation.

1.33–1.35

Read the interface, verify the breath, and reassess

Frequency
Set mandatory respiratory rate.
Tidal volume or pressure
Controls the size or driving pressure of supported breaths, depending on mode.
FiO₂ and inspiratory time
Set oxygen concentration and timing.
Alarms
Define conditions requiring immediate assessment.

Week 1 clinical takeaways

  1. Airflow requires a pressure gradient and always moves from higher to lower pressure.
  2. PIP includes elastic and resistive pressure; plateau pressure isolates the elastic component when flow is zero.
  3. Use exhaled tidal volume for static compliance and convert flow from L/min to L/s for airway resistance.
  4. Compliance and resistance combine to determine how quickly lung units fill and empty.
  5. A widening PIP–plateau gap suggests increased resistance; both pressures rising together suggests decreasing compliance.
  6. Trace gas from machine to patient and back, verify the circuit and pre-use test, and confirm that the machine, circuit, and patient findings agree.
